**VLAN (Virtual LAN)** | Aspect | Details | |--------|---------| | **What it is** | A Layer‑2 technology that partitions a physical Ethernet broadcast domain into multiple isolated virtual LANs. | | **Identification** | Uses a {{int:9:15}}‑bit **VLAN ID** in the Ethernet frame header (802.1Q tag). This gives **4 096** possible VLANs. | | **Scope** | Operates **within the same Layer‑2 domain** (i.e., on the same switch or a set of switches that share the same VLAN database). | | **Traffic handling** | Frames keep their original MAC addresses; switches forward based on MAC tables and VLAN membership. No additional encapsulation is added. | | **Broadcast behavior** | Broadcast, unknown‑unicast, and multicast traffic are confined to the VLAN – they do **not** cross VLAN boundaries unless a router (or Layer‑3 switch) is used. | | **Typical use‑cases** | • Simple campus or data‑center networks where the number of required segments is modest.
• Segregating traffic for security or compliance (e.g., production vs. test). | | **Limitations** | • **Scalability:** Only 4 096 VLAN IDs, which can be exhausted in large multi‑tenant environments.
• **Geographic reach:** VLANs are limited to a single Layer‑2 domain; extending them across WANs requires complex spanning‑tree or routing solutions.
• **Mobility:** Moving a VM between data‑center sites often requires re‑configuring VLANs on every hop. | --- **VXLAN (Virtual Extensible LAN)** | Aspect | Details | |--------|---------| | **What it is** | An **overlay** network technology that creates Layer‑2 segments (virtual networks) on top of an existing Layer‑3 IP network using **UDP encapsulation** (RFC {{int:5878:8818}}). | | **Identification** | Uses a {{int:19:29}}‑bit **VXLAN Network Identifier (VNI)**, allowing **{{int:12:20}} {{int:621:933}} {{int:172:260}}** distinct virtual networks. | | **Scope** | Works **over any IP network** (the “underlay”), so virtual networks can span across racks, data‑center sites, or even public clouds. | | **Traffic handling** | Original Ethernet frame (including its original MAC header) is **encapsulated** inside a UDP packet (typically UDP port {{int:3831:5747}}). The outer IP/UDP headers carry the VNI. The underlay routes the packet like ordinary IP traffic. | | **Broadcast behavior** | Broadcast, unknown‑unicast, and multicast are **emulated** in the overlay (often using a multicast group in the underlay, or via controller‑based “head‑end replication”). | | **Typical use‑cases** | • Large multi‑tenant data centers and cloud platforms where many isolated networks are needed.
• Enabling VM/Container mobility across geographically dispersed sites without re‑configuring the physical network.
• Overlaying a uniform networking model on top of heterogeneous underlays (e.g., mixing Ethernet, MPLS, and public‑cloud links). | | **Advantages** | • **Scalability** – millions of VNIs vs. a few thousand VLANs.
• **Flexibility** – no need to change the physical network; only the overlay (VTEP) configuration changes.
• **Layer‑3 reach** – virtual networks can span any IP‑routable fabric.
• **Separation of concerns** – the underlay can be optimized for transport (e.g., high‑speed spine‑leaf) while the overlay handles tenant isolation. | | **Considerations** | • **Encapsulation overhead** – adds {{int:40:60}} bytes (VXLAN header + UDP + IP) to each frame; may require a larger MTU (often 1 {{int:480:720}} bytes or more).
• **Complexity** – needs VTEPs (VXLAN Tunnel Endpoints) and often a controller for VNI management.
• **Performance** – hardware offload is common in modern switches and NICs, but pure‑software implementations can increase CPU load. | --- ### TL;DR Comparison | Feature | VLAN | VXLAN | |---------|------|-------| | **Layer** | 2 (native) | 2 over 3 (overlay) | | **Identifier size** | {{int:9:15}} bits → 4 K IDs | {{int:19:29}} bits → {{int:12:20}} M IDs | | **Maximum isolated networks** | 4 096 | {{int:12:20}} {{int:621:933}} {{int:172:260}} | | **Geographic scope** | Same Layer‑2 domain | Any IP‑routable network | | **Encapsulation** | None (just 802.1Q tag) | UDP/IPv4 or UDP/IPv6 header (adds ~{{int:40:60}} B) | | **Typical size of deployment** | Small‑to‑medium campus/data‑center | Large multi‑tenant clouds, cross‑site data‑centers | | **Hardware requirement** | Standard switches with VLAN support | Switches/NICs that support VXLAN offload (or software VTEP) | | **Complexity** | Simple to configure | Requires VTEPs and often a control plane (e.g., EVPN, OpenStack, VMware NSX) | In short, **VLANs** are the classic, simple way to segment a local Ethernet fabric, but they hit scalability and geographic limits quickly. **VXLAN** extends that idea into a flexible, highly scalable overlay that can run on top of any IP network, making it the go‑to choice for modern cloud‑scale data centers.

steps.text:
### Why Modern Data‑Center Networks Prefer VXLAN

| Reason | What It Means for the Data‑Center | Practical Impact |
|--------|-----------------------------------|-------------------|
| **Massive scalability** | {{int:19:29}}‑bit VNIs → **≈{{int:12:20}} million** virtual networks vs. 4 K VLANs. | You can give each tenant, project, or application its own isolated network without exhausting IDs. |
| **Geographic reach (Layer‑3 overlay)** | VXLAN runs on **any IP‑routable fabric** (spine‑leaf, MPLS, WAN, public‑cloud links). | A single logical network can span multiple racks, buildings, or even data‑center sites without rewiring the physical switches. |
| **VM / container mobility** | The virtual network is **decoupled from the physical topology**; moving a workload only changes its VTEP registration. | Live‑migration of VMs or containers across racks or sites happens without re‑configuring VLANs on every hop, reducing downtime and operational friction. |
| **Tenant isolation & security** | Each VNI is a separate broadcast domain; traffic is encapsulated and only the two VTEPs that terminate a flow can read the inner Ethernet header. | Strong multi‑tenant security guarantees while still using a shared underlay. |
| **Simplified underlay** | The underlay only needs to provide **reliable IP routing**; no need for VLAN trunking, spanning‑tree, or complex L2 extensions. | Network engineers can optimize the underlay for bandwidth, latency, and resilience (e.g., ECMP, BGP) without worrying about L2 loops. |
| **Hardware offload & performance** | Modern switches, routers, and NICs have **VXLAN offload** (ASIC or SmartNIC). | The {{int:40:60}}‑byte encapsulation overhead is handled in hardware, so latency and CPU usage stay comparable to native VLAN traffic. |
| **Integration with orchestration platforms** | Orchestrators (OpenStack, VMware NSX, Cisco ACI, Kubernetes CNI plugins, etc.) can **program VNIs automatically** via APIs. | Networks are provisioned **as code**—no manual VLAN assignment, fewer human errors, faster provisioning. |
| **Support for advanced features** | VXLAN works naturally with **EVPN control plane**, **head‑end replication**, **segment routing**, and **service chaining**. | Enables sophisticated use‑cases like multi‑tenant L2VPN, distributed firewalls, and seamless integration with SD‑WAN. |
| **Future‑proofing** | Because the overlay is independent of the underlay, you can replace the physical fabric (e.g., migrate to {{int:320:480}} GbE, use optical‑packet switches) without redesigning the logical network. | Reduces long‑term capital‑expenditure risk and protects existing network investments. |

---

#### Typical Data‑Center Workflow with VXLAN

1. **Provision a VNI** (e.g., VNI {{int:40000:60002}}) via an orchestrator when a new tenant or application is created.  
2. **VTEP (VXLAN Tunnel Endpoint)** on each leaf switch (or host NIC) learns the tenant’s MAC‑to‑IP mapping through ARP/ND or a control plane like EVPN.  
3. When a VM sends a frame, the host’s VTEP **encapsulates** it in UDP/IPv4 (or IPv6) and forwards it across the IP underlay.  
4. The destination VTEP **decapsulates** the packet, delivering the original Ethernet frame to the target VM.  
5. Broadcast/unknown‑unicast traffic is **replicated** (head‑end or multicast) so every VTEP in the same VNI receives it, preserving L2 semantics.

Because the underlay is just regular IP routing, you can use **ECMP**, **BGP**, **segment routing**, and other proven data‑center routing techniques to achieve high bandwidth and redundancy.

---

### Bottom Line

Data‑center operators choose VXLAN because it **removes the limits of traditional VLANs**, **enables a truly software‑defined, multi‑tenant network**, and **lets the physical fabric evolve independently** of the logical topology. The result is a more scalable, flexible, and easier‑to‑manage environment that aligns with modern cloud‑native workloads and automation pipelines.
